# Bioresorbable Vascular Scaffolds in Percutaneous Coronary Intervention: A Narrative Review

## Introduction and rationale

Permanent metallic drug-eluting stents (DES) revolutionised percutaneous coronary intervention (PCI) but carry intrinsic long-term limitations. The permanent presence of a metal stent prevents coronary vasomotion, autoregulation, and adaptive coronary remodeling. Drug-eluting metallic coronary stents predispose to late stent thrombosis, prevent late lumen vessel enlargement, hinder surgical revascularisation, and impair imaging with multislice CT. Bioresorbable vascular scaffolds (BVS) were conceived to overcome these constraints [1,2]. Bioresorbable polymeric drug-eluting scaffolds were developed as an alternative to metallic drug-eluting stents with the aim of providing transient vessel support combined with drug delivery capability without the long-term limitations of permanent metallic stents. Devices are constructed from either bioresorbable polymers or biocorrodible metal alloys [3].

## First-in-human experience and early trials

The first-in-human ABSORB Cohort A study evaluated a poly-L-lactic acid (PLLA) everolimus-eluting BVS. We assessed the safety of the bioabsorbable everolimus-eluting stent. 30 patients with a single de-novo coronary artery lesion were followed up for 2 years clinically and with multiple imaging methods. [4,5]. These encouraging signals prompted larger randomised comparisons against the cobalt-chromium everolimus-eluting stent (EES, Xience).

The ABSORB II trial provided the first randomised comparison [6]. Patients were randomly assigned in a 2:1 ratio to receive treatment with an everolimus-eluting bioresorbable scaffold (Absorb; Abbott Vascular, Santa Clara, CA, USA) or treatment with an everolimus-eluting metallic stent (XIENCE; Abbott Vascular). Subsequent regulatory trials—ABSORB China, ABSORB Japan, and ABSORB III—were designed to support approval in their respective markets [7,8,9]. The primary end point is target lesion failure (the composite of cardiac death, target vessel-related myocardial infarction, or ischemia-driven target lesion revascularization) at 1 year, powered for noninferiority of ABSORB BVS compared to XIENCE EES. A patient-level pooled meta-analysis confirmed comparable 1-year outcomes [10]. On this basis, BVS received approval and were widely adopted: BVS obtained FDA approval for US marketing and have been widely implanted around the world, with more than 100,000 BVS deployed.

## Emerging safety signals

Longer follow-up tempered initial enthusiasm. The pivotal ABSORB III trial established 1-year non-inferiority, but between 1 and 3 years and cumulative to 3 years, adverse event rates (particularly target vessel myocardial infarction and scaffold thrombosis) were increased after BVS [11,12]. The all-comers AIDA trial reported early because of safety concerns [13]. In this preliminary report of a trial involving patients undergoing PCI, there was no significant difference in the rate of target-vessel failure between the patients who received a bioresorbable scaffold and the patients who received a metallic stent. The bioresorbable scaffold was associated with a higher incidence of device thrombosis than the metallic stent through 2 years of follow-up. The five-year ABSORB II results were unfavourable [14]: the advantage of a bioresorbable scaffold over a metallic stent was not demonstrated, suggesting that an improved version of the bioresorbable scaffold is needed to justify its clinical use.

A three-year individual-patient-data meta-analysis quantified the excess risk [15]. BVS compared with cobalt-chromium everolimus-eluting stents resulted in higher 3-year rates of target lesion failure (11.7% versus 8.1%; risk ratio [RR], 1.38; 95% confidence interval [CI], 1.10–1.73; P=0.006). Meta-analyses consistently identified an excess of scaffold thrombosis across early, late, and very-late time windows [16,17,18]. Network meta-analysis showed that patients treated with the Absorb bioresorbable vascular scaffold (BVS) had a significantly higher risk of definite or probable scaffold thrombosis (ScT) compared to those treated with metallic DES. The risk of very late ScT was highest with the Absorb BVS. Contributing mechanisms included thick struts, malapposition, and underexpansion [19].

## Time-varying outcomes and the resorption hypothesis

A central question is whether the risk-benefit balance changes after complete resorption at ~3 years. The five-year ABSORB III analysis and pooled studies suggest the hazard is confined to the bioresorption period [20,21]. The final ABSORB-program report pooled five trials [22]: Between 0 and 5 years, TLF occurred in 15.9% BVS patients vs 13.1% EES patients (HR: 1.25; 95% CI: 1.08-1.43; P = 0.002), and DT occurred in 2.2% vs 1.0%, but the period of excess risk ended at 3 years, the time point of complete scaffold bioresorption.

## Optimised technique and ABSORB IV

Recognising that procedural technique drives early events, the ABSORB IV trial mandated optimised implantation [23,24]. Polymeric BVS implanted with optimised technique in an expanded patient population resulted in non-inferior 30-day and 1-year rates of target lesion failure and angina compared with metallic DES. The COMPARE-ABSORB trial in high-restenosis-risk patients showed a more cautionary picture [25]. A randomized trial comparing the bioresorbable vascular scaffold to the everolimus-eluting metallic stent in 1670 high-risk patients found non-inferiority for the primary endpoint of target lesion failure at 1 year but higher risks of early thrombosis and myocardial infarction with the bioresorbable scaffold. Registry data such as FRANCE ABSORB echoed a similar temporal pattern [26].

## Next-generation devices

Attention has shifted to thinner-strut and metallic resorbable platforms [27]. The higher scaffold thrombosis rates observed with the first-generation bioresorbable scaffolds (BRSs) compared to conventional drug-eluting stents were likely due in part to bioresorbable polymers having insufficient radial strength, necessitating larger strut profiles. The magnesium-based DREAMS programme produced the Magmaris scaffold (BIOSOLVE-II) and the third-generation DREAMS 3 (BIOMAG-I) [28,29], while iron-based and other sirolimus-eluting platforms remain investigational [30].

## Conclusions

First-generation polymeric BVS failed to deliver the anticipated late clinical advantage over contemporary DES and were withdrawn from routine practice owing to excess thrombotic risk during the bioresorption window. The lessons—optimal sizing, lesion preparation, postdilatation, thinner struts, and prolonged dual antiplatelet therapy—are informing a new generation of devices. Whether refined scaffolds can match the early safety of DES while delivering genuine late benefit remains to be proven in adequately powered long-term trials.
